note: The all-purpose reaction to anything impressive or shocking. You will hear it constantly.

example.en: No way! Really?

note: A short gasp of surprise or disbelief. Typed constantly in messages.

example.en: Whoa, when did that happen?

note: Honey is used as a prefix meaning "great". The opposite is 노잼.

example.en: This drama is so much fun.

note: The English "no" glued to 재미. Blunt but not rude.

example.en: That film was boring.

note: Someone who is naturally in the middle of things. The opposite is 아싸, an outsider.

example.en: She is totally the social type.

note: An abbreviation of 갑자기 분위기 싸해짐. Used when a joke lands badly.

example.en: My joke killed the mood.

note: English "king" as an intensifier stuck onto 열받다. Playful rather than serious anger.

example.en: Ugh, that is so annoying.

note: A shortening of the English phrase. Handy when there is no single answer.

example.en: It depends on the person.

note: Very common online and often written JMT. The first syllable comes from a vulgar word, so keep it away from work and older people. 정말 맛있어요 is the safe version.

example.en: This place is unbelievably good.

lit: what are you going to do + TV
note: A teen taunt with no real meaning attached to the TV part. Fine as a joke between friends, dismissive to anyone else.

example.en: Yeah, whatever.

note: A prefix that stamps something as genuine — 찐 맛집 is a place that actually deserves the hype. Also used alone as agreement: "찐."

example.en: This place is the real deal.

note: Waking early, studying, exercising, ticking boxes — and posting the routine. Half aspiration, half joke about how hard it is to keep up.

example.en: These days I am living the disciplined life.

note: A gym-selfie caption and hashtag. Say it out loud and people will know exactly which app you learned Korean from.

example.en: Workout done! Went to the gym again today.

lit: from 손절매, cutting your losses on a stock
note: Ending a friendship or a relationship on purpose, the way a trader dumps a losing share. Blunt, so use it about your own life, not someone else’s.

example.en: I cut that person off.

note: Appears in group chats around 11:30 every day. The reply is usually a photo of someone else’s lunch.

example.en: Recommend me a lunch, someone!

en: A disaster you brought on yourself
lit: 스스로 불러온 재앙, "a calamity you called down on yourself"
note: Said with a sigh about your own bad decision — the all-nighter, the third coffee, the impulse purchase.

example.en: I watched dramas all night — my own doing.

en: Iced Americano, no matter the weather
lit: 얼어 죽어도 아이스 아메리카노, "iced Americano even if I freeze to death"
note: The most-used piece of slang in a 2026 survey. Describes the huge tribe of Koreans who order iced coffee in January. Say it about yourself and any barista will smile.

example.en: I am an iced-Americano person — even in winter.

en: What matters is not giving up
lit: 중요한 건 꺾이지 않는 마음, "the important thing is a heart that does not bend"
note: Born at the 2022 World Cup and still everywhere — exam season, sports, job hunting. Safe with anyone; older people know it too.

example.en: I failed once, but I am not giving up!

lit: 이게 왜 진짜?, "why is this real?"
note: A three-syllable gasp at news that sounds like a joke but is not. Typed under viral posts more than said out loud.

example.en: That actor is getting married. Wait, that is real?

en: Lucky me — look on the bright side
lit: lucky + Vicky, IVE member Jang Wonyoung’s English name
note: From a clip in which she called a setback lucky. Used with a wink whenever something goes wrong and you decide it was for the best. Jokey; not for a real crisis.

example.ko: 비 와서 집에서 쉬네. 완전 럭키비키잖아
example.en: It is raining, so I get to rest at home. Lucky me!

en: The look or vibe you are going for
note: The style and image you aspire to, as opposed to what you look like on a Monday. Common in fashion, beauty and idol talk: “my 추구미 is clean and quiet.”

example.en: The look I am going for is clean and simple.

en: A sudden crash back to reality
note: The moment after the fun — the empty delivery boxes, the credit-card bill, the 3 am scroll — when you see your life clearly and wince. Everyday word in twenties and thirties talk.

example.en: Now that I have shopped, reality is hitting me.

note: Something so standard it counts as law — fried chicken with beer, ramyeon after drinking, a selfie at the top of the mountain. Heard from teens to office workers; fine in most company.

example.en: Beer with fried chicken — that is the rule.

note: The two-syllable caption under a photo of a cafe, a street or an outfit that just looks right. Written far more than spoken; older people may need it explained.

example.en: This cafe has such a nice vibe.

note: From football commentary — a player in crazy form — now said about idols, actors, a friend’s new haircut or your own good week. 미쳤다 (“crazy”) is a compliment here, but it is slangy, so not for the office.

example.en: That actor is on absolute fire lately.

en: To hold on and wait it out
lit: a crude intensifier + 버티다, "to hold out"
note: Started with stock and crypto traders refusing to sell, now used for anything you grimly sit through. The first syllable is from a vulgar word, so it stays in chat and among friends — 버티다 or 기다리다 is the safe version.

example.en: Even if the stock drops, I am holding on.

lit: a pun: 사귀다 (to date) sounds like “four”, so one step before it is “three”
note: The stage of texting every day and going out together without either person saying the word. Teens and twenties only; anyone older will hear “사귀다” and get confused.

example.en: We are still in the almost-dating stage.

note: A normal dictionary word turned into a one-word reply that means “yep, true.” Online it is typed as just the consonants ㅇㅈ, and as a question — 인정? — it asks “agreed?”. Fine with anyone your age; a little casual for a boss.

example.en: This place is really good, right? — Fair enough.

note: The too-bright energy of someone performing excitement they do not feel — a variety-show host, a group chat, you at a work dinner. The honest opposite is 찐텐, real energy. Note that 텐션 in Korean means your energy level, not stress.

example.en: That reaction was totally forced.

en: Just handle it well, no instructions needed
lit: 알아서 잘 딱 깔끔하고 센스있게, "on your own, well, neatly and with good sense"
note: Five words crushed into five syllables. Said half as praise for someone who needs no briefing, half as an unreasonable request. A boss who says this to you has told you nothing.

example.en: Just take care of it nicely, you know how.

lit: 별걸 다 줄인다, "they abbreviate even the odd things"
note: The complaint about all the slang on this list, and itself an abbreviation — which is the joke. Handy for a learner: say it and Koreans will laugh and then explain the word you missed.

example.en: You shorten everything — what does that even mean?

note: Korea argues about mint chocolate ice cream the way other countries argue about pineapple on pizza. 민초단 is the tribe that loves it; 반민초단 the resistance. A safe, cheerful thing to have an opinion about.

example.en: I am on team mint choc.

en: Running a joke into the ground
lit: brain + a severing, from a manga move done one time too many
note: The fourth time someone repeats the same gag. Used as a verb — 뇌절하다 — or thrown at someone mid-repetition. Mildly cutting, so keep it among friends.

example.en: That joke is worn out now.

note: Said when something goes wrong and you decide out loud that it worked out. Plain words, so it is safe with anyone; the slang is in the timing, right after the bad news.

example.en: The plan fell through. Honestly, better this way.

en: Are you a robot or what?
lit: "are you a T?" — the Thinking type in MBTI
note: Thrown at someone who answers a sad story with practical advice instead of sympathy. Koreans talk about MBTI types constantly, and T versus F (Feeling) is the classic split. Teasing, not an insult — but only with friends.

example.ko: 나 감기 걸렸어 — 병원 가. — 너 T야?
example.en: I caught a cold. — Go see a doctor. — Wow, so cold.

lit: 내 돈으로 내가 산, "bought by me with my money"
note: Stamped on reviews and posts to promise they are not sponsored. When you are hunting for honest restaurant or skincare reviews on Naver or Instagram, this is the tag to search for.

example.en: This is an unsponsored review — I bought it myself.

lit: 꾸민 듯 안 꾸민 듯, "dressed up, or maybe not"
note: The look that took forty minutes to make appear accidental. Used for clothes, make-up and even cafe interiors. A compliment — say it about someone’s outfit and they will be pleased.

example.en: You look effortlessly good today.

note: A playful, cutesy way to call food tasty, often as a noun: “this is a 맛도리”. Teens and twenties use it in food vlogs and comments; it sounds childish coming from a manager.

example.en: This tteokbokki is so good.

lit: origin debated; it simply means shabby or second-rate
note: For anything that feels low-effort or embarrassing — a cheap-looking set in a drama, a tacky gift, a desperate excuse. Not crude, but it is a put-down, so be careful who it lands on.

example.en: The CGI in that drama was kind of cheap.

note: Young people loving old-fashioned things: injeolmi, sweet potato, black sesame, red-bean desserts, floral patterns. You will see it on cafe menus advertising “할매니얼 디저트”.

example.en: My taste in food is totally grandma.

en: A something — the stage before dating
note: Two people clearly like each other but nobody has said so yet. 썸 타다 is to be in that stage; endless drama plots live here.

example.en: We’re in that in-between stage.

note: Once slightly shameful, now completely normal — restaurants have single seats for it. 혼술 is the drinking version.

example.en: I had lunch on my own today.

note: Showing interest, then pulling back to keep the other person guessing. Usually said with mild disapproval.

example.en: Stop playing hot and cold.

note: Staring into space doing absolutely nothing. Treated as a skill here — Seoul holds a competition for it by the river.

example.en: I just sat by the river and zoned out.

note: The standard compliment for a cheap place that is good. 가심비 is the version where it only has to make you happy.

example.en: This place is good value.

en: A meal you have arranged with someone
note: Campus slang, usually a senior student taking a junior out to eat. 술약 is the same thing with drinking.

example.en: I’m meeting an older student for a meal.

lit: 아주 보통의 하루 (a very ordinary day)
note: Picked by the Trend Korea 2025 book and now all over SNS captions. The happiness of a quiet, unremarkable day — the opposite of showing off.

example.en: Today was just a nice, ordinary day.

note: The healthy-living trend of eating and sleeping so you age more slowly — think brown rice and fewer sugary drinks. You will see it on menus and in convenience-store aisles.

example.en: I’m on a slow-ageing diet these days.

en: A bold, take-charge kind of guy
note: A 2025 personality label: direct and assertive. Its opposite is 에겐남, from estrogen, for a gentle, sensitive man; women get 테토녀 and 에겐녀. Mostly a joke, like MBTI.

example.en: You’re such a take-charge guy.

note: Reading books, writing by hand and posting about it as a style statement. Bookshop visits and reading-club photos are the typical posts.

example.en: My vibe these days is the bookish look.

note: Started around 2015 as a compliment for youthful people in their forties, but now usually said mockingly. Many find it ageist, so do not call someone this to their face.

example.en: That outfit looks a bit try-hard forty.

note: From the six-sided stat charts in games: looks, money, job, personality, health and family all maxed out. Usually said with envy or as a joke.

example.en: That senior is good at literally everything.
